text.p: **BIRTHDAYS**
Dutch painter, REMBRANDT VAN RIJN, whose most famous picture was "The Night Watch", was born in 1606.
Australian newspaper editor, THOMAS GARRET, who founded the 'Illawarra Mercury', was born in 1830. He entered parliament but was rejected as a Cabinet Minister due to his alcoholism.
Australian rugby league footballer, STEVE MORTIMER, was born in 1956.
**EVENTS**

1099 : Jerusalem was seized by Christian Crusaders, who massacred the Jewish and Muslim citizens. The city had been under Muslim rule since the seventh century. The capture of the ancient city was part of the first armed pilgrimage organised by

1908 : A new football competition, the newly-formed professional Rugby League, was launched in Sydney. The League was born after a Rugby Union dispute over expenses to cover injured players. The competition attracted eight teams.
1912 : New ski chalets at Mt Kosciusko and Mt Buffalo were reportedly attracting holiday makers to the once "remote Great Dividing Range."
British novelist, IRIS MURDOCH, whose works included "A Severed Head" and "The Good Apprentice", was born in 1919.
One of Australia's most married women, SUSAN ROSSITER-PEACOCK-SANGSTER-RENOUF, was born in 1942.

American singer, LINDA RONSTADT, who began her career with a family folk trio, was born in 1946. In 1964 she formed the 'Stone Poneys' and went solo in 1968. Her hits included "You're No Good" (1974),"When Will I Be Loved" (1975), "Blue Bayou" (1977) and "Don't Know Much" (1989).
Pope Urban II to recapture places sacred to Christians.
1795 : The 'Marseillaise' was officially adopted as the French national anthem.
1904 : Russian dramatist, ANTON CHEKHOV, who wrote major plays such as "The Cherry Orchard" and "The Three Sisters", died.
1913 : In London, a woman wearing a split skirt was arrested for indecency.
1930 : The British government ordered 1,000 Spitfire fighter planes.
1938 : Millionaire HOWARD HUGHES set a new world record for a round-the-world flight. It took just three days, 19 hours and 17 minutes.
1945 : The lights went on again all over Britain for the first time in 2,000 nights, after the ending of the war-time black-outs.
1954 : The new Boeing 707 made its maiden flight from Seattle.
1964 : A new national newspaper, RUPERT MURDOCH's "The Australian" was published for the first time.

1973 : PAUL GETTY III, the teenage grandson of oil tycoon, PAUL GETTY, was kidnapped. He was freed by his Italian kidnappers six months later, after they cut off his right ear and sent it through the mail to reinforce their demand for a $750,000 ransom.

1977 : Anti-drug campaigner, DONALD MACKAY, disappeared in suspicious circumstances in the New South Wales town of Griffith. His car was found in a hotel car park, with three spent .22 cartridges and a pool of blood nearby. Police suspected mafia-style gunmen had flown out from the deserted
Griffith airport, after shooting MACKAY.
1989 : Eleven people were killed and 127 injured in clashes between Georgians and Abkhazians in Soviet Georgia.
1990 : In Sri Lanka, Tamil Tigers massacred 168 Muslims.
1994 : Former West Australian Premier BRIAN BURKE was sentenced to two years jail after being convicted of fraud charges, relating to travel expenses.
